title: Carvedilol and Alcohol: Coreg CR, Dizziness, and Safe Timing
excerpt: Can you drink on carvedilol (Coreg)? How alcohol and carvedilol lower blood pressure together, the Coreg CR two-hour rule, heart failure cautions, and warning signs.
metaDescription: Can you drink on carvedilol? Why alcohol and Coreg cause dizziness, the Coreg CR two-hour rule, heart failure cautions, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** some people who take carvedilol (brand name Coreg) are allowed an occasional drink by their doctor, but only your prescriber can say whether that includes you, and how much. But carvedilol is not a typical beta blocker. On top of slowing your heart, it also relaxes and widens your blood vessels. Alcohol widens blood vessels too. Put the two together and the most common result is dizziness, light-headedness, or fainting, especially when you stand up. The extended-release capsule (Coreg CR) has a second, separate issue: alcohol can make the capsule release its drug faster than designed, so the prescribing information tells you to keep alcohol away from your dose by about two hours on either side.

**The quick rules:** Never skip, delay, or stop a carvedilol dose so you can drink. Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound, and the label carries a boxed warning about it. If you take Coreg CR, don't drink alcohol (or take liquid medicines that contain alcohol) within roughly two hours before or after your capsule. Take immediate-release carvedilol with food, as directed. Keep drinks light and slow, drink water alongside, and stand up slowly, particularly in the first weeks after starting or changing your dose. If you take carvedilol for heart failure, ask your cardiologist directly how much, if any, alcohol is right for you, because the answer is often "less than you think."

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how carvedilol and alcohol interact in general terms. It is not a substitute for advice from the doctor or pharmacist who knows your heart condition, your dose, and your other medicines. **Talk to your doctor before drinking on carvedilol if** you take it for heart failure, you've had a heart attack, you've fainted or nearly fainted since starting it, you have diabetes, or you take other blood pressure medicines. **Call 911 or go to the emergency room if** you faint, have chest pain, have a very slow or irregular heartbeat with dizziness or shortness of breath, or develop sudden swelling, wheezing, or trouble breathing.

## How Carvedilol and Alcohol Interact: The Mechanism in Plain Words

To understand why this pairing can make you dizzy, it helps to know what carvedilol actually does. Most beta blockers, such as metoprolol and atenolol, mainly do one thing: they block the "speed up" signal that adrenaline sends to your heart. That slows the heart rate and reduces how hard the heart pumps.

Carvedilol does that too, but it also blocks a second type of receptor, called alpha-1, that sits on the walls of your blood vessels. Alpha-1 receptors are what tighten your blood vessels when you need to keep blood pressure up, for example when you stand. Blocking them lets the vessels stay relaxed and open. That's part of why carvedilol works so well in heart failure, since it lowers the resistance the heart has to pump against. It's also why dizziness when standing is one of its best-known side effects.

Now add alcohol. In the short term, alcohol also relaxes and widens blood vessels, which is why your face can feel warm and flushed after a drink. So for a few hours you have two things opening up your blood vessels at once, and one of them (carvedilol) is also stopping your heart from speeding up to compensate.

Normally, when you stand up, gravity pulls blood toward your legs, and your body reacts within seconds by tightening blood vessels and nudging the heart rate up. On carvedilol plus alcohol, both halves of that reflex are dulled. The result can be a sudden drop in blood pressure when you stand, called orthostatic hypotension, which feels like a head rush, tunnel vision, a wobbly feeling, or, at worst, fainting.

### Why carvedilol may be touchier than other beta blockers here

Because of its extra alpha-blocking effect, carvedilol tends to cause more standing-up dizziness than beta blockers that only act on the heart. Its own prescribing information warns about low blood pressure and fainting, especially after the first dose and after dose increases, and advises people to sit or lie down if they feel dizzy. Alcohol stacks on top of exactly that weakness. If you've switched from a different beta blocker and alcohol never bothered you before, don't assume it will feel the same on carvedilol.

### The longer-term clash

The short-term effect of alcohol is to lower blood pressure, but regular heavier drinking does the opposite over weeks and months. It's one of the best-established lifestyle causes of high blood pressure, and it can trigger heart rhythm problems such as atrial fibrillation. In people with heart failure, heavy drinking can weaken the heart muscle directly. So the more you drink on a regular basis, the more you're working against the reason carvedilol was prescribed in the first place. For more on that side of the picture, see our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025).

## Coreg CR and Alcohol: The Two-Hour Rule

This is the part of the carvedilol and alcohol story that most articles skip, and it only applies to one version of the drug.

Carvedilol comes in two main forms:

- **Immediate-release tablets** (Coreg and generic carvedilol), usually taken twice a day with food.
- **Extended-release capsules** (Coreg CR, carvedilol phosphate), taken once a day, usually in the morning with food.

An extended-release capsule is engineered to let the drug out slowly over the whole day. The Coreg CR prescribing information states that alcohol can interfere with that design and cause the capsule to release carvedilol faster than intended. This is sometimes called "dose dumping." If more of the dose arrives in your bloodstream at once, you'd expect stronger effects in the hours that follow: a bigger drop in blood pressure, a slower heart rate, and more dizziness.

The practical instruction from the label is to avoid drinking alcohol, and to avoid medicines that contain alcohol, for about two hours before and after taking Coreg CR. "Medicines that contain alcohol" is the easy one to miss. Some liquid cold and cough syrups, some mouthwashes you might swallow by accident, and some herbal tinctures contain alcohol. Check the label or ask a pharmacist.

For most people on Coreg CR this is easy to arrange. If you take your capsule with breakfast, an evening drink is far outside the window. The risky situations are things like taking a late-morning dose at a brunch with mimosas, or taking a forgotten dose late in the evening right before or after a drink. If you've missed a dose and you've been drinking, don't double up later. Ask a pharmacist what to do with that specific dose.

### Does the two-hour rule apply to regular carvedilol tablets?

The dose-dumping warning is specific to the extended-release capsule, because it's about how the capsule's slow-release design behaves in alcohol. Immediate-release tablets don't have that design. The general dizziness and blood pressure interaction still applies to both forms, though, so spacing a drink away from your dose and having it with food is a sensible habit with either one. Your pharmacist can tell you which version you have if you're not sure. The bottle label will say "CR" or "ER" for the extended-release form.

## Can You Drink on Carvedilol? Who Should Be Most Careful

There isn't one answer for everyone, because carvedilol is prescribed for quite different reasons. The reason you take it matters more than the drug itself.

**If you take it for high blood pressure** and your numbers are well controlled, your doctor may be fine with some alcohol. If so, ask them to set the amount, since it depends on your heart, your other medicines, and how you react to carvedilol. Less is better for blood pressure, and spacing drinks out matters more than people realize.

**If you take it for heart failure**, be more cautious. Alcohol can weaken the heart muscle, add fluid and salt (think beer and salty bar food), and interact with the other heart failure medicines you're likely taking, such as diuretics. Some cardiologists advise people with heart failure to avoid alcohol completely, especially if their heart failure was caused or worsened by drinking. Others allow small amounts. This is a conversation to have with your own cardiologist, not a rule to guess at.

**If you take it after a heart attack**, the same applies. Ask your cardiologist what's safe for your situation.

**Other people who should talk to a doctor first:**

- People in the first few weeks after starting carvedilol or after a dose increase, when dizziness is most common.
- Older adults, who are more prone to dizziness on standing and more likely to be hurt by a fall.
- People with diabetes (more on this below).
- People who take other medicines that lower blood pressure, such as amlodipine, lisinopril, losartan, diuretics, or nitrates, or medicines for erectile dysfunction. Every extra blood-pressure-lowering drug adds to the stack. If you're on amlodipine as well, our [amlodipine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/amlodipine-and-alcohol) covers that piece.
- Anyone who takes sleeping pills, anxiety medicines, opioids, or other sedating drugs, since alcohol and these together can slow breathing and reaction time.

## How Much Can You Drink on Carvedilol?

No official dose of alcohol is "safe on carvedilol," and nobody can give you a universal number without knowing your heart condition. What you can do is reduce the chance of feeling unwell:

1. **Start low after any change.** If you've just started carvedilol or had your dose raised, skip alcohol for the first week or two, and ask your doctor before restarting, until you know how the drug feels on its own.
2. **Eat first.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, and immediate-release carvedilol is meant to be taken with food anyway.
3. **Alternate with water.** Alternate each alcoholic drink with a glass of water. Dehydration lowers blood volume, and lower blood volume makes the standing-up blood pressure drop worse.
4. **Go slowly.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot from person to person. Drinking faster than that lets alcohol build up.
5. **Stand up in stages.** Sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a moment before standing, especially at night and the next morning.
6. **Avoid heat stacking.** Hot tubs, saunas, and hot days widen blood vessels too. Drinking in a hot tub while on carvedilol is a recipe for a faint.

## How Long After Taking Carvedilol Can You Drink?

**For Coreg CR,** the label guidance is about two hours on either side of your dose. Most people take it in the morning, so an evening drink is well clear.

**For immediate-release carvedilol,** there's no official waiting time. Carvedilol's effect on blood pressure peaks a few hours after each dose, which is when dizziness is most likely. If you want to be cautious, avoid drinking right around your dose and have your drink with a meal. What you should not do is shift, skip, or delay a dose to make room for drinking. Taking it consistently matters more than timing it around alcohol.

**How long after your last drink can you take carvedilol?** Take your next dose on schedule. If you drank heavily and feel very dizzy, faint, or unwell when the dose is due, call your doctor, a pharmacist, or a nurse line for advice rather than skipping it on your own.

## Never Skip a Dose to Drink

This deserves its own section because it's the most dangerous mistake people make. Some people think, "I'll skip tonight's carvedilol so I can have a few drinks." Don't.

Carvedilol, like other beta blockers, has a boxed warning against stopping it suddenly. When the drug is withdrawn abruptly, the heart can become extra sensitive to adrenaline. In people with coronary artery disease, this has been linked to worsening chest pain, heart attack, and dangerous rhythms. In people with heart failure, missing doses can let symptoms flare. One skipped dose is not the same as stopping the drug for weeks, but deliberately skipping doses around drinking is a habit that adds risk for no benefit. If you're going to drink, take your carvedilol as usual and drink less.

## Carvedilol, Alcohol, and Low Blood Sugar

If you have diabetes, especially if you use insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide, there's an extra layer to consider.

Alcohol can lower blood sugar, sometimes many hours after you stop drinking, because the liver is busy processing alcohol instead of releasing stored sugar. At the same time, beta blockers like carvedilol can hide some of the classic warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a racing heartbeat and shakiness. Sweating is usually not blocked, so it can be a useful clue.

Practical steps if you have diabetes:

- Never drink on an empty stomach.
- Check your blood sugar before bed after drinking, and have a snack with some carbohydrate if your doctor recommends it.
- Make sure the people you're with know that confusion or slurred speech could be low blood sugar rather than drunkenness.
- Talk to your doctor about how alcohol fits with your diabetes medicines.

## The Carvedilol Hangover: Why the Morning After Can Feel Worse

People on carvedilol often notice that hangovers hit differently. A few reasons:

- **Dehydration and low blood pressure.** Alcohol makes you urinate more, which lowers your blood volume. On a drug that already widens blood vessels, that can mean more dizziness when you get out of bed. Stand up slowly and rehydrate first thing.
- **Tiredness.** Fatigue is one of carvedilol's common side effects, and alcohol wrecks sleep quality. The two together can make the next day feel heavier.
- **Blunted heart rate response.** Many people get a racing heart after drinking. Carvedilol may dampen that, which some people find reassuring. But if your heart feels like it's fluttering, skipping, or beating irregularly, that's not a hangover symptom to ignore, as alcohol can trigger atrial fibrillation even in people on beta blockers. Our guide to [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains what's normal and what isn't.

For hangover pain, check with your pharmacist before reaching for ibuprofen or naproxen. Anti-inflammatory painkillers can raise blood pressure and cause the body to hold onto fluid, which is a particular concern for people with heart failure. Acetaminophen is often the preferred choice for people with heart conditions, but it has its own alcohol cautions, covered in our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol).

## Carvedilol vs Other Beta Blockers With Alcohol

If you're comparing notes with friends or family on different beta blockers, here's how carvedilol fits in:

- **Metoprolol and atenolol** mainly act on the heart. They can still cause dizziness with alcohol, but generally they're less likely to cause the standing-up blood pressure drop that carvedilol's alpha-blocking effect adds. See our [metoprolol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/metoprolol-and-alcohol) for details.
- **Propranolol** is an older beta blocker that acts on both the heart and other tissues and is often used for anxiety, tremor, and migraine. It has its own considerations, covered in our [propranolol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/propranolol-and-alcohol).
- **Carvedilol and labetalol** both block alpha receptors too, so they share the stronger blood-vessel-widening effect.

For a side-by-side view of the whole class, see our [beta blockers and alcohol hub](/never-hungover/beta-blockers-and-alcohol).

## Warning Signs: When to See a Doctor

Mild light-headedness that passes when you sit down is common and usually not an emergency. But some symptoms are not something to sleep off.

**Call 911 or go to the emergency room if you or someone with you:**

- Faints or can't stay standing.
- Has chest pain, pressure, or tightness.
- Has a very slow heartbeat along with dizziness, confusion, or shortness of breath.
- Has a fast, pounding, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle.
- Develops sudden swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or trouble breathing.
- Becomes confused, very drowsy, or hard to wake.

**Call your doctor soon if you notice:**

- Dizziness on standing that keeps happening, even without alcohol.
- New or worsening swelling in your ankles or legs, sudden weight gain over a few days, or getting short of breath lying flat. These can be signs of heart failure getting worse.
- Frequent low blood sugar episodes if you have diabetes.
- You find it hard to keep to the limit your doctor set. That's worth raising simply because regular heavier drinking works against your heart treatment.

## What About DHM and Other Hangover Supplements?

If you're reading this because you want to enjoy a night out without feeling terrible the next day, it's reasonable to wonder whether supplements can help. Here's the honest picture.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers reliably in people, and it does nothing to change the carvedilol and alcohol interaction. It won't stop the blood pressure drop, it doesn't make the Coreg CR two-hour rule optional, and it doesn't make heavier drinking safe for your heart.

There's also little research on DHM in people taking heart medicines. Some lab work suggests DHM might affect liver enzymes that process drugs, though what that means in people is unclear. If you take carvedilol and want to try DHM, show the product label to your pharmacist or cardiologist first. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known.

If your doctor is comfortable with it, commonly chosen options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. Avoid hangover products that contain stimulants or high doses of caffeine, and check any "electrolyte" product for high sodium if you have heart failure and are on a salt limit.

The most effective hangover strategy on carvedilol is still the simple one: fewer drinks, more water, food first, and standing up slowly.

## The Bottom Line

- Carvedilol both slows the heart and widens blood vessels. Alcohol widens blood vessels too, so the combination's main risk is dizziness and fainting, especially when standing.
- For **Coreg CR**, the prescribing information warns that alcohol can make the capsule release its drug too quickly. Keep alcohol, and alcohol-containing medicines, about two hours away from your dose on either side.
- **Never skip or stop a dose to drink.** Sudden withdrawal is dangerous.
- If you take carvedilol for **heart failure** or after a **heart attack**, ask your cardiologist how much alcohol, if any, is right for you.
- If you have **diabetes**, alcohol can cause low blood sugar and carvedilol can hide some of its warning signs.
- Light, slow drinking with food and water, and standing up in stages, keeps most people out of trouble. Heavy or regular drinking works against the reason you take carvedilol.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking carvedilol?**

Some people are allowed an occasional drink by their doctor, but it depends on why you take carvedilol, so ask yours first. Alcohol and carvedilol both widen blood vessels, so the main risk is dizziness or fainting, especially when standing. People with heart failure or a recent heart attack should ask their cardiologist first, as many are advised to limit alcohol strictly or avoid it.

**Why can't you drink alcohol with Coreg CR?**

The Coreg CR prescribing information states that alcohol can cause the extended-release capsule to release carvedilol faster than intended. That could lead to a stronger drop in blood pressure and heart rate. The label advises avoiding alcohol, and medicines that contain alcohol, for about two hours before and after your dose.

**How long after taking carvedilol can I drink alcohol?**

For Coreg CR, wait about two hours after your dose, and don't drink in the two hours before it. For immediate-release carvedilol there's no official waiting time, but having your drink with food and away from the hours right after your dose may reduce dizziness. Never move or skip a dose to make room for drinking.

**Is it OK to skip a carvedilol dose if I'm going to drink?**

No. Carvedilol carries a boxed warning against stopping it suddenly, because withdrawal can worsen chest pain and, in some people, trigger a heart attack or dangerous rhythm. Take your dose as usual and drink less instead. If you're unsure about a specific dose, ask a pharmacist.

**Does alcohol make carvedilol side effects worse?**

It can. Alcohol can intensify carvedilol's most common side effects, especially dizziness, light-headedness, and tiredness. The effect tends to be strongest in the first weeks after starting carvedilol or after a dose increase, in older adults, and in people who take other blood pressure medicines.

**Can I drink alcohol with carvedilol if I have heart failure?**

Ask your cardiologist. Alcohol can weaken the heart muscle and add fluid and salt, and people with heart failure usually take several medicines that interact with it. Some doctors advise avoiding alcohol completely, especially if drinking contributed to the heart failure. Others allow small amounts.

**Is carvedilol worse with alcohol than metoprolol?**

Carvedilol may cause more dizziness with alcohol for some people, because it also blocks alpha receptors on blood vessels, letting them widen further. Metoprolol mainly acts on the heart. Both can still lower blood pressure with alcohol, so the same cautions apply: drink lightly, eat first, and stand up slowly.

**Does DHM interact with carvedilol?**

There's little research on DHM in people taking carvedilol or other heart medicines, and DHM doesn't change the carvedilol and alcohol interaction. Some lab studies suggest DHM may affect drug-processing liver enzymes, but the meaning for people is unclear. Check with your pharmacist or cardiologist before combining them.
